articles.title: PNP conducts operation vs Bantag at Ifugao poultry farm
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said an operation was conducted to arrest former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 11:29am

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said an operation was conducted to arrest former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on Sunday.
However, Bantag was not found at the location during the operation.

“Police conducted an operation at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on November 1 after receiving information that Bantag was hiding there and posing as a poultry worker,” the PNP said in a statement.
“However, he was not found at the location,” it added.
The PNP said it remains committed to pursuing Bantag, who is wanted over his alleged involvement in the 2022 killing of broadcaster Percival Mabasa or "Percy Lapid."
PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio C. Nartatez Jr. said authorities would continue their efforts to serve the warrant against Bantag.
“We will not allow the passage of time or repeated attempts to evade arrest to weaken our resolve. The PNP will remain relentless in pursuing those who are wanted by the law,” Nartatez said.
“Every lead will be pursued, every lawful opportunity will be acted upon, and we will not stop until they are brought before the courts to answer for the charges against them,” he added.
Nartatez described the recent operation as proof of the police force's determination to locate and arrest wanted individuals.
“This is not a setback but a proof that we remain relentless in locating and arresting him as well as other high-profile fugitives,” he said.
The PNP also called on the public to provide information that could help authorities locate Bantag and other wanted individuals.

In April 2023, a Muntinlupa Regional Trial Court court ordered the arrest of Bantag in connection with the death of Jun Villamor, the alleged middleman in the killing of broadcaster Percy Lapid in October 2022.
Bantag has denied the allegations against him.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) previously said a P2-million reward would be given for information leading to Bantag’s arrest. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Bantag allegedly disguised as poultry worker, not found during Ifugao police operation
articles.summary: Fugitive former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag has eluded arrest in Ifugao, according to the mayor of Lamut, Ifugao.

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 11:19am
The place where former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag allegedly eluded arrest on the early morning of Nov. 1, 2026.
Mariano B. Buyagawan Jr. / Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Fugitive former Bureau of Corrections Chief Gerald Bantag has eluded arrest in Ifugao, according to the mayor of Lamut, Ifugao.
In a Facebook post, Lamut Mayor Mariano Buyagawan Jr. said Bantag was hiding at a local poultry farm, where he allegedly disguised himself as a poultry worker.

“So what is a fugitive General doing? He was not hiding in the mountains. Not in a cave. Not in another country. He was hiding inside the poultry farm in Pugol! Wearing slippers! Holding a balde (bucket) of chicken feeds! Pretending to be a poultry boy!” Buyagawan said in a Facebook post on Sunday, November 1.
According to Buyagawan, police raided the farm at 5 a.m. on Sunday.
The Police Regional Office - Cordillera (PRO-CAR) also confirmed that an operation to arrest Bantag had been conducted.
PRO-CAR said that the operation was carried out by personnel from the Ifugao PPO and the 1501st Regional Mobile Force Battalion 15.
“However, the operation yielded no arrest, as the subject of the warrant was not present in the area during implementation,” the PRO-CAR said.
However, contrary to Buyagawan’s claim, PRO-CAR said Bantag did not evade arrest because he was not present in the area during the operation.

“PRO-CAR clarifies that no arrest was made because the subject was not present at the identified location when police personnel conducted the operation. Thus, the claim that the subject eluded arrest is not true,” it said.
Police urged the public “to remain vigilant and cooperate with law enforcement authorities by providing credible information that may help locate wanted persons.”

Bantag is facing murder charges in connection with the killings of broadcaster Percy Lapid and inmate Jun Villamor, as well as corruption-related complaints over the alleged misuse of funds for prison projects.
His alleged accomplice, Denver Mayores, was sentenced to two to eight years in prison for his role in Lapid’s killing.

articles.title: Binance sees outflows stabilising as exchange returns online after $6.3-billion heist
articles.summary: The Binance theft, which analysts say could be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts

blocks.text: BINANCE. Representations of cryptocurrencies are seen in front of displayed Binance logo in this illustration taken November 10, 2022.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The Binance theft, which analysts say could be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts

items: Binance experienced $3.64 billion in withdrawals, representing 2.1% of its assets, following a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in $6.3 billion being stolen.
The exchange has reassured investors by stabilizing withdrawals and covering 95% of the stolen assets, while also implementing phased withdrawals based on user demand.
The FBI attributed the attack to a North Korean state-sponsored unit, and Binance committed to covering the financial losses from the hack using company funds.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion stolen from the platform last week.

The exchange moved to reassure crypto investors and said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. It said it had now covered 95% of the assets stolen in the heist.

After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday. Ether hit a two-month low on Friday and also recovered a little to $2,287.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally. It said on Sunday it had $171 billion in total assets under management as of October 28.
“(That) puts the withdrawals in the range of a precautionary reaction rather than any sort of capital flight,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs.

The Binance theft, which analysts say could be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust Binance with their money after the attack.

Stablecoin market capitalisations tend to fall when money is leaving cryptocurrencies and they have dropped since Friday. The combined capitalisation of the two largest stablecoins, USDT and USDC, has dropped by about $1.2 billion since Friday, according to Coinmarketcap.com.

Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in stages, prioritising user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin.
“We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand,” Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.
It added, “Rest assured that market conditions are stable.”

Binance said earlier on Sunday it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may take longer to source in the required amounts, it said.

Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited after the event. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboardthat outflows were higher, at $5.81 billion, up from the $4.36 billion it showed earlier. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updated figures.

“This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted),” a spokesperson for Binance said of the initial DefiLlama data.
The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.

Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.

Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected “further laundering” of the assets through the use of related technology.

Analysts had also pointed to North Korea’s involvement. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
US President Donald Trump, however, later on Saturday said it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved.
“We don’t know if it’s North Korea — but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it,” Trump told reporters in comments posted by a White House account on X.
Binance said it will bear the financial impact of the hack and has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses.

The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance’s $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.

Co-CEO Yi He said on the weekend Binance would use 50% of its SAFU funds, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 billion. She warned Binance had been made aware of new scams that had emerged during the past few days “amid the chaos”. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bicam talks on 2027 budget to be opened to CSOs -- JV Ejercito
articles.summary: Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 10:31am

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.

Just like last year, Ejercito also confirmed that the bicameral deliberations which would reconcile the Senate and the House of Representatives’ differing versions of the budget bill, would also be livestreamed to allow the public to watch the proceedings in real time.
“We are continuing to build on our best practices. This year, we will be inviting CSOs to sit in and observe the bicameral proceedings,” the senator said in a statement.
“Having more eyes on the budget will help us spot any unvetted projects or last-minute insertions that may be introduced during the bicam,” he added.
Last Monday, October 26, the Senate panel conducted a dedicated hearing with CSOs to discuss their recommendations and concerns on the 2027 budget.

During the hearing, the People's Budget Coalition (PBC) cautioned against over a trillion worth of “red flags” under the proposed budget. These reportedly covered various types of “pork” or discretionary funds under the House General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

House leaders, on the other hand, defended the amendments made by the chamber to the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these were purportedly based on agency proposals and had been made on valid grounds.
Ejercito maintained that he wants to ensure that every single peso in the 2027 budget would be “accountably and transparently allocated.”
He also invited the public to use the digital tools developed by CSOs in reviewing budget documents and flagging questionable allocations.

“Transparency is not just a policy statement, it is an active mechanism. These tools were built by watchdogs themselves, and we are glad to give them a home on the Senate website so ordinary citizens can scrutinize where public funds are going,” Ejercito said.
The Senate Finance panel is currently finalizing its committee report, with Ejercito set to formally sponsor the 2027 General Appropriations Bill on the floor this month. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests
articles.summary:
Deployments of surveillance vans over five months result in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders

  • Get our

blocks.text: More than a million people have had their faces scanned in a trial of real-time facial recognition technology in Western Australia, resulting in 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts.
WA police said under the five-month trial, which concluded on Saturday, the technology scanned 1,380,882 faces after 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations.
Alongside the 122 arrests, the alerts led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders and locate 10 people for a welfare check.
The deployments included three operations at the Perth Royal Show, where 223,749 faces were scanned, resulting in 15 alerts, three arrests and seven “interactions” with registered sex offenders.
A police spokesperson confirmed the system generated nine incorrect alerts against the total 1.38m scans, meaning there was an error rate of 0.00065%.
Addressing the false matches at a media conference on Sunday, the WA police commissioner, Col Blanch, confirmed officers engaged with each individual.
“I want to be very clear on those false alerts,” he said. “No one was arrested. No one made a complaint. Each one did result in an interaction with that person and asking them relevant questions.

“It’s a very, very, very low number. It’s not zero. We’d love it to be zero. But I think the important thing for us is to engage with our community just like we would if a human thought someone was a wanted person.”

Blanch acknowledged the technology was “not perfect” and that authorities “knew this going into this trial”, but maintained that officers followed up on alerts in the same way they would if a member of the public raised suspicions.
However, civil liberties advocates have criticised how the WA police framed the error rate.

The chief executive of Civil Liberties Australia, Bill Rowlings, said WA police were “severely gilding the lily” by claiming the incorrect alert rate was 0.00065% and suggested it should instead be calculated by comparing how many of the arrests resulted in convictions.
“We will only know what the incorrect rate is when the 122 people arrested have their day in court,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
“If half the 122 arrested … are not convicted, the ‘incorrect’ rate will be 50%,” he said in a statement, saying police had performed the almost 1.4m scans “with no reasonable suspicion whatsoever”.

When the trial was announced, the state’s independent privacy watchdog, the Office of the Information Commissioner WA (OIC WA), said it was not involved in implementing the trial, warning of “collective privacy harms” in a statement. The OIC WA was contacted for comment.

blocks.caption: The police surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the trial is evaluated. Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAP

blocks.text: On Sunday, Blanch said the trial “focused on using modern technology responsibly to identify people who presented a risk, while allowing the vast majority of people to go about their day without any impact”.

Under the trial guidelines, cameras mounted on or positioned near marked police vehicles scanned faces in designated public areas, matching them against an alert list drawn from police databases. Police said images of people who weren’t on the list were pixelated in real time and deleted immediately without being stored.

The trial previously triggered backlash over concerns about privacy and algorithmic bias. Experts say the technology could disproportionately affect marginalised groups who are already overrepresented on police watchlists, with facial recognition algorithms historically having higher false-match rates for people with darker skin tones.

The surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the force conducts an internal evaluation into how the technology performed on the ground and its community impacts, including “reviewing the safeguards and whether all requirements were met”.

articles.title: House spends P100M a year on utilities. Why ask for P1B?
articles.summary: In 2025, the House secured a billion pesos for the chamber's water and electricity expenses, even though it historically spent only a small fraction of that amount annually. Where did the money go?

items: The House of Representatives has consistently requested inflated budgets for utilities and supplies, despite underspending significantly in these areas, raising concerns about the utilization of unspent funds.

Critics, including Congressman Toby Tiangco, have highlighted the lack of transparency in the House's budget allocation and spending, suggesting that unused funds may be redirected to extraordinary expenses without proper oversight.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

In the last five years, the House’s utility expenses averaged only P108 million per year, but the chamber keeps on requesting — and approving — an inflated budget, never mind if it has already reached a billion pesos.
The underspending is a total head-scratcher, especially because it becomes uncertain how the eventual savings are being utilized.
The House enjoys fiscal autonomy, which means that unlike other government agencies, it is not required to return unspent funds to the Bureau of Treasury.
In the absence of transparency, critics warn that the funds may be prone to abuse and corruption.
Take a look at the 2025 budget of the House of Representatives, the latest of which has been subject to complete state auditing.

The General Appropriations Act — signed by the President after it was approved separately by the House and the Senate — gave the House a total of P1.35 billion for the chamber’s water and electricity expenses.
The Commission on Audit’s report, however, learned that the chamber spent only over one-tenth of its actual utility allocation.

Did the House anticipate a major spike in utility needs for 2025 that it needed a gargantuan budget for power and water? They didn’t say so, but trends show that the House has had a habit of securing an inflated utility budget, even though it only needs a small fraction of the funds.
The underspending goes beyond utilities.
The House’s budget for supplies has also tremendously increased in recent years, from P327.98 million in 2021, to a whopping P1.34 billion in 2025.
That’s even though spending for supplies averaged only P83 million annually in that half-decade.

blocks.caption: Graphics by David Castuciano/Rappler

blocks.text: Where did the savings go? Finding out was Congressman Toby Tiangco’s agenda when he interpellated the budget sponsor of the Commission on Audit (COA) during plenary debates in the House.
“COA’s job is to audit what was spent, what is being spent. COA doesn’t know where the savings went,” said COA budget sponsor in the House, Representative John Tracy Cagas.
For Tiangco, the practice of budget allocation does not make sense.
“Why is there high funding for supplies and utilities but are left unspent, and then the following year, you still increase the budget?” Tiangco told Rappler.
Tiangco’s suspicion is that savings from utilities and supplies are being realigned to extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses (EME).

EME cover unique demands not typically covered by standard budgets. The Department of Budget and Management says these refer to expenses incurred for meetings, seminars, public relations, and official entertainment, among other things. EME should not be used for salaries, wages, allowances, and confidential expenses.

Following those guidelines to the dot may be easier said than done. A 2011 concurrent resolution by Congress states that these funds — which fall under maintenance and other operating expenses (MOOE) — require liquidation only by way of certification.
In other words, no official receipts are needed to justify these expenses.

“Unused funds of the House don’t revert to the Treasury. However, the House Speaker can declare those unused funds as savings as provided under the Constitution and relevant General Provisions on use of savings in an annual GAAs,” budget expert Zyza Suzara told Rappler.
“These savings are typically used to provide hefty bonuses for congressional staff of the House of Representatives,” she added.

The disparity between the allocated extraordinary funds for the House and its actual expenditure is astonishing. In 2025, the overspending reached P3.74 billion. The question arises: where did the extra funds come from?
Transparency on the MOOE allocated to every congressman has been among Tiangco’s recent crusades. COA, after all, has confirmed that the MOOE for districts are not the same.

Tiangco has been a thorn in the House majority during the budget process this year. He wrote to Speaker Bojie Dy in August, informing him of his decision to break ranks and become an independent, to allow him “greater latitude to raise questions…in the use of public funds.”

This is not the first time Tiangco parted ways with the majority. Close and longtime observers of the House budget process may not find it uncharacteristic of Tiangco to be a champion of budget accountability, but given his background — particularly his perceived kinship to his relative, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. — his vocal opposition to the budget proposal may come across as jarring.
Tiangco, alongside over a dozen lawmakers, voted against the 2027 spending bill approved by the House, citing the chamber’s supposed rejection of his proposed transparency reforms.
His demands are a tough ask anyway. For one, he wanted the budget of the House of Representatives to undergo actual scrutiny.

This meant a public committee hearing for the House’s 2027 appropriations, pegged at P17.6 billion. Tiangco later said the House revised the executive’s proposal and increased its own appropriations by P5 billion for the upcoming fiscal year.

The House in recent memory has not conducted committee deliberations on its own budget. The free pass is similar to what’s been given to the Office of the President, the Supreme Court, and the Office of the Vice President before Sara Duterte parted ways with the Marcos administration.

A proper committee hearing, or even plenary-level debates, could have provided clarity on various questions surrounding the House’s expenditures, including its underspent utilities and supplies funding.
Rappler has emailed Speaker Dy’s office for comment. We will update this story once we receive a reply.

blocks.caption: WATCH: Why the budget process of Philippine Congress is prone to corruption

blocks.text: Since the House’s approval of the 2027 budget, the chamber has faced greater scrutiny after budget watchdogs crunched the numbers and found that the chamber included nearly P190 billion in public works funding despite the absence of published project attachments.

In simple words, the House appears to have modified the President’s budget proposal so much that it resulted in hundreds of millions to billions of pesos in insertions in congressmen’s respective districts.

Even Tiangco’s constituency isn’t spared. The tracker of People’s Budget Coalition and Better Gov says that P338 million in insertions were made to the district engineering office covering Malabon and Navotas, raising its total funding to P1.12 billion.

Tiangco has disclosed a P2.28-billion public works funding for Navotas, up from the P1.61 billion that he said was included in the executive’s original proposal. But Tiangco insists the increase is backed by project details, and is in line with what the Regional Development Council and civil society organizations originally approved for his city.

blocks.caption: How to track insertions in House-approved 2027 budget

blocks.text: But the seeming top offender for the 2027 budget is no less than the President’s son himself, Majority Leader Sandro Marcos. The DPWH engineering office in the Ilocos Norte district he represents has been allocated P4.74 billion in public works projects, up from the P369 million that was originally proposed by the executive.
In short, the House has increased his district’s budget by P4.38 billion. The younger Marcos has not provided an explanation for the budget adjustment.
The staggering figures underscore the alarming need for transparency. The watchdogs based their analysis on figures from engineering offices, but they sometimes cover numerous constituencies.
This means that the exact allocation per congressional district, and the insertions made by party-list lawmakers, cannot be fully determined, unless the House opens up its books to the public.
But does the House really have the guts — or decency — to truly pierce its longstanding veil of secrecy? – Rappler.com

Police believe most or all of the objects, which also included metal screws, were placed intentionally to cause harm.
Incidents were reported in Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, and Rhineland-Palatinate, among other locations, police said.
In one of the cases in the southern city of Nuremberg, police said a child had bitten down on a needle while eating a piece of chocolate. The child was unharmed.

In several of the cases, police have opened investigations into attempted aggravated assault.

articles.title: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.summary:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards

Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico,…

blocks.text: Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.

Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.

The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.

The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms, but polls have let them down before
articles.summary: Polls have been predicting a Democratic surge, but last-minute deciders and sampling issues mean there's no guarantee.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
By
North America correspondent
The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.

Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.

A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.
But are the polls accurate?

Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.

Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.

According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."

If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.

While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.

It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.

The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeat

blocks.text: Obama gives a press conference the day after the heavy 2010 midterms defeat
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.

Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.

At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.

The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
Voter voices: What issues matter most to Americans?
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.

Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.
"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally
articles.summary:
President again took aim at progressive Senate candidate and lauded Haley Stevens for endorsing Mike Rogers

Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a…

blocks.text: Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”.
Trump’s comments aimed to influence a neck-and-neck race that will play an outsized role in determining which party controls the senate after Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected.
“If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump said.

The Michigan race has drawn national attention in recent days, as Hayley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the August primary election, declined to campaign with him, while demanding that he publicly disavow an outside group’s political ad that posited a link between rising prices and US military support for Israel’s war on Gaza.

El-Sayed responded by telling Stevens to stay away from a campaign event at which they were supposed to appear together on Sunday. Stevens turned around and endorsed Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent. Steven’s high-profile defection in the waning hours of the tight race drew the condemnation of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, who is Jewish.
Trump, on the other hand, heaped praise on Stevens for turning against El-Sayed, urging her to join the GOP.
“It was an incredible thing,” Trump said. “I’d love her to join the Republican party. I think that could happen.”
Trump then lauded Rogers in metaphorical terms.
after newsletter promotion

“Mike Rodgers is apple pie,” Trump said. “And you know what this country needs? A little apple pie. We don’t need the communists or jihadists, the Muslim Brotherhood. We need apple pie. He’s apple pie. He’ll be good.”
Trump had little time to watch football this weekend, he noted, because he had been “going to these damn rallies all over the place”.
“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump said. “Essentially, I am on the ballot.”

articles.title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
articles.summary: There were hundreds of arrests as protesters took to the streets in cities across France for the third weekend in a row.

blocks.text: Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.

An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.

Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.

The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."

Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.

French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".

France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.

Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

articles.title: Nearly 1.2 million passengers monitored at ports so far amid Undas 2026 --PCG
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard has monitored nearly 1.2 million passengers at ports nationwide as of Monday morning, November 2, amid the influx of travelers during the Undas 2026 long weekend.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 8:03am
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) has monitored nearly 1.2 million passengers at ports nationwide as of Monday morning, November 2, amid the influx of travelers during the Undas 2026 long weekend.
PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said port operations have generally been smooth despite several maritime incidents reported in recent days.
“As we speak, halos 1.2 million na po ang pasaherong ating na-monitor sa lahat ng pantalan,” Cayabyab told Unang Balita in an interview.
(As we speak, we have already monitored almost 1.2 million passengers at all ports.)

The passenger count is still lower than the approximately 1.5 million recorded during the same period last year. However, Cayabyab said the PCG expects the number to increase as Oplan Biyaheng Ayos remains in effect until Tuesday, November 3.
A surge of returning passengers is expected on Monday, particularly after lunch, according to the PCG official.
Arrive early
Cayabyab reminded the public to purchase tickets early and arrive at ports ahead of their scheduled departure to allow sufficient time for security inspections.
“Iwasang magdala ng mga pinagbabawal na mga items, 'yung matulis, flammable, explosive kasi definitely bawal pong isakay 'yan sa ating sasakyang pandagat,” she said.
(Avoid bringing prohibited items, such as sharp, flammable, explosive items, because these are definitely not allowed on board our vessels.)
“At palagi pong sumunod sa mga instructions, particularly 'yung pagsusuot po ng life jacket para masigurado po ang ating kaligtasan,” she added.
(And always follow instructions, particularly, wearing a life jacket to ensure our safety.)
Meanwhile, the PCG is investigating the near-sinking of motor banca M/B Rose Marie One off Dalupiri Island in Calayan, Cagayan, on Saturday, October 31.

“Ang naging reason ng insidente base sa report na natanggap natin, may mga sakay itong livestock. So may tendency kasing gumalaw ito sa loob ng kanyang motorbanca. Pero may nabuksan na isang parang close na ano sa may cargo area. So ito 'yung nag-cause ng pagpasok ng sea water,” she said.

(The reason for the incident, based on the report we received, was that there were livestock on board. So these had a tendency to move around inside the motorbanca. But something that looked like a closed door in the cargo area opened so this is what caused the sea water to enter the vessel.)
She said the incident was reported early so the Coast Guard responded immediately and rescued the crew members. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine air raid app apparently hacked as users receive false radiation threat, Air Force says
articles.summary: Authorities say there is no threat and have advised the public to stay calm and follow official channels for information.

blocks.text: Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The Air Force message on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."

The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said on Telegram that there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation regarding the threat of air strikes.
The messages, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next alert, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."

articles.title: Parents of woman who died of seizure after ChaGPT misguidance sue OpenAI
articles.summary:
Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage

A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice…

blocks.text: A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents to sue OpenAI earlier this week.
The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately led to their death.
In this case, Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Chinese software engineer living in Seattle, sought advice from ChatGPT after Amazon fired her, according to the lawsuit.

She needed to find a new job to obtain permanent residency and was concerned that her anti-seizure medication, Lamotrigine, was impeding her ability to speak English. She needed the language skills for interviews.

The bot, communicating in Chinese, provided her a tapering schedule to reduce her 400mg dose to zero, a regimen no physician had prescribed, the lawsuit states. ChatGPT told her the tapering made it “highly likely” that she would be able to regain her ability to speak English.
The bot also told her to avoid her physicians and encouraged “medical freedom over obeying the doctor”, the complaint states.
Before an appointment, with a primary care physician, the bot stated, “Do not mention Lam reduction plan.”

While reducing her medication, she started experiencing symptoms of focal seizures. Wan asked the bot if she needed to worry about brain damage. The tool reassured her that she did not and that what she had experienced was not a seizure, the lawsuit alleges.

She continued to suffer seizures, but the bot told her to keep tapering her medication. On 12 February this year, she died from a seizure. Her parents, who were in China, had not heard from her so they flew to Seattle and found her dead on 14 February, the lawsuit states.
The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI could have prevented Wan’s death, but failed because it had not built the proper safeguards into the bot when it communicated in Chinese.
OpenAI could have programmed the bot to issue “a categorical warning to every prompt” Wan sent, the suit stated. For example, “I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider.”
Wan’s parents are seeking damages for her death and to prevent OpenAI from practicing medicine “without a license on the users of their products”.
An OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, told the New York Times that Bowen’s story was “an incredibly heartbreaking situation” but that Wan used a version of ChatGPT that was no longer available.
Newer versions are better at recognizing when a matter needs urgent attention, Pusateri said.

“While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals,” Pusateri told the Times.

Others have also alleged that OpenAI is responsible for their loved ones’ suicides. Several lawsuits concern cases in which the bot encouraged teens to kill themselves and provided guidance on how to do so.
In response to some of those cases, an OpenAI spokesperson in 2025 also called the deaths an “incredibly heartbreaking situation”.

articles.title: Plane carrying 9 people crashes in Florida neighbourhood
articles.summary: A business jet carrying nine people nosedived into a South Florida neighbourhood on Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway,…

image.caption: Emergency crews respond to a plane crash in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday. (Mark Elias/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A business jet carrying nine people nosedived into a South Florida neighbourhood on Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway, creating a giant fiery crater in the pavement.
It's not immediately clear if fiery crash led to injuries, deaths
It was not immediately known if anyone on the Learjet 60 or on the ground in the Palm Beach County neighbourhood was injured or killed.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
A message seeking comment was left with officials at the airport in Texas.

Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.

The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.
A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for about two hours following the crash. The circumstances of the crash remained under investigation.

articles.title: Nationals leader Matt Canavan to run for lower house seat in possible showdown with One Nation’s James Ashby
articles.summary:
Tilt comes after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, will run in a lower house Queensland seat at the next federal election, in a move that may see him face off with Pauline Hanson’s chief of staff.
The announcement follows the retirement of the Capricornia MP Michelle Landry, and could result in a contest against James Ashby in a major battle for regional seats.
“The issue is we need to keep this seat to change the government, and I want us to continue to deliver for central Queensland,” Canavan told the Courier-Mail on Monday.
“I don’t think you’ll be surprised by this announcement but I’m not going to die wondering. I may very well die politically, but I’m not going to die wondering. I’ll give it my all.”
Landry, based in Rockhampton, announced her decision last month to retire from politics and not to recontest her seat at the next election.
The Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie said One Nation should not be fighting to win Coalition-held seats if the party was serious about taking on Labor.
“If One Nation is really serious about firing the liar, then they need to start running in Labor party seats instead of running against someone like Matt Canavan,” she told Nine’s Today show.
“[I’m] not afraid of a fight – I want to save our country, and that means changing the prime minister, and that means taking Labor party seats.”
after newsletter promotion
More details soon …

articles.title: Doerkson says 'preference' is for B.C. public servants to return to office work
articles.summary: British Columbia's incoming premier says his "preference" is to see teleworking public servants return to the office environment.

image.caption: B.C.'s premier-designate has left the door open to some hybrid work arrangements, but says his preference is for public servants to return to the office. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: British Columbia
British Columbia's incoming premier says his "preference" is to see teleworking public servants return to the office environment.
Premier-designate acknowledged some form of hybrid work arrangements will likely persist
But in a wide-ranging interview on his government's priorities, B.C. Conservative Leader and Premier-Designate Lorne Doerkson left the door open for flexibility on remote work.
"I think there is probably always going to be a hybrid sort of feature going forward," Doerkson said.
"But certainly my interest would be having people come back for sure."
Federal public servants back in the office 4 days a week
In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, B.C.'s public service opted to officially retain flexible and work-from-home arrangements in a bid to attract a greater variety of workers.
In 2023, it announced that all public service jobs would be open to "any B.C. community where the hiring ministry has an existing office," and support flexible and remote work arrangements.
At the time, public service head Shannon Salter said the idea was to recruit employees who work everywhere in the province, not just Vancouver and Victoria.

That contrasts with provinces like Alberta and Ontario, which have recently mandated a return to full-time, in-office work. Federal public servants were directed to return to the office four days a week in July.
B.C. General Employees Union president Paul Finch told CBC News that he was "a bit concerned" by Doerkson's comments.
Finch said remote work has been a cost-saving measure for the province, allowing it to reduce its real estate footprint and recruit workers at a lower cost in communities with a lower cost of living.
"It also really benefits a lot of small town B.C.," Finch said.

"You have a lot of civil servants working remotely in smaller communities, and they're a key economic driver in those communities. We are talking about former resource communities that no longer have that inflow of money."
What’s on the horizon as B.C. Conservatives take the reins after 9 years of NDP rule
Finch said the union welcomes a conversation about changes to remote work, but said any changes should be deliberate and cautious.
"We will have those conversations," Doerkson said when asked about public sector workers in rural and remote communities.
"But my preference would be obviously coming back to workplaces."
Doerkson is expected to be sworn in later this month, after the provincial election results are finalized on Nov. 18.
With files from Katie DeRosa

articles.title: Business jet carrying nine people crashes in Florida neighborhood
articles.summary:
It is unclear if anyone on the ground was hurt and no details yet on whether anyone onboard survived

A business jet carrying nine people crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday, erupting…

blocks.text: A business jet carrying nine people crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday, erupting in a massive fireball.
The Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area in Florida’s Palm Beach county, federal officials said.
The Bahamas-bound jet departed from Austin-Bergstrom international airport in Texas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.
It was unclear if anyone on the ground was hurt. There were also no details yet on whether anyone onboard survived.

Video of the crash showed the aircraft nose-diving from the sky and then erupting into a giant ball of flames near a major roadway, only inches from passing vehicles. The crash left a giant crater in the pavement with flames leaping up from it near a utility pole.

Chunks of pavement were seen in the footage engulfed in fire as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes. Black smoke billowed out of the hole, wafting past palm trees swaying on the stormy day.

articles.title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final
articles.summary:
Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity

A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in…

blocks.text: A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.
The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.
The 18-year-old is from Leicestershire, and in her first year of undergraduate studies at the Royal Academy of Music.

The brainchild of Humphrey Burton, the biennial BBC competition was set up in 1978 and has produced finalists such as Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Alison Balsom, Stephen Hough and, in 2004, Nicola Benedetti, who was the last violinist to win.

Demetriades was one of several hundred to send in a video application, before 40 young players were selected to attend live auditions in Bath Spa University to gain one of eight places in the quarter-finals – which took place on Demetriades’ 18th birthday. Among her fellow quarter-finalists was the first accordion player to reach the final stages, 14-year-old Sylvester Maschi.

blocks.caption: Recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni, violinist Sofia Demetriades and saxophonist Kezia Colton, finalists of BBC Young Musician 2026. Photograph: BBC/Betsan Evans

blocks.text: Each of the three finalists performed a concerto with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alpesh Chauhan in a concert at Bristol Beacon. An 18-year-old saxophone player, Kezia Colton, performed Takashi Yoshimatsu’s 1994 Cyber Bird Saxophone Concerto, while 17-year-old recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni played Graham Fitkin’s Recorder Concerto.

Fitkin’s virtuosic concerto involves six different recorders, ranging from the giant contrabass, about 1.6 metres high, to the tiniest sopranino. It was originally commissioned by Debretzeni’s teacher, Barbara Law, and it was given its premiere performance in 2017 by 2014’s Young Musician finalist, Sophie Westbrooke. And there was a further connection this year to previous competitions – 2022’s overall winner, the percussionist Jordan Ashman, joined Kezia Colton onstage for Yoshimatsu’s concerto.
“Kezia plays with incredible verve and spirit, said Wallen. “Her performance was sassy and cool,” said Gernon, “but her more intimate playing is incredibly strong too.”
The judges hailed the “electricity, aliveness, and beautiful intensity” that Debretzeni brought to Fitkin’s concerto. “She took us on a musical journey … we were inside every note,” said Wallen.

“Before the competition I hadn’t planned on being a musician,” said Debretzeni. “I wanted to study psychology … but this has been so inspiring it’s made me want to pursue music. It’s been literally life-changing.”
Demetriades was acclaimed as a simply extraordinary musician by MacGregor. “She performs with her eyes, achieving dizzying technical feats but she looks as if she’s enjoying it,” she said.

“Sofia’s innate sense of colour, musical style and architecture combines with an effortless technique, and a joy for whatever music she’s playing. In a competition full of gifted and dedicated young musicians, Sofia’s sensitivity and sophistication stood out in every round. I’m very excited to watch her musicianship develop even further in the years ahead.”

The winner receives the trophy, a cash prize of £3,000 towards music studies as well as recording and broadcast opportunities on Radio 3, including with one of the BBC ensembles. All three finalists will work with Young Classical Artists Trust on managing their future careers.

“I am so honoured and thrilled to have been a part of BBC Young Musician,” said Demetriades. “I loved playing in the quarter-final on my 18th birthday. I didn’t think I could top that, but to go on to be crowned winner is my absolute dream! It was pure delight to share the stage with BBC NOW, Alpesh Chauhan and my fellow finalists – I really hope to play alongside them again soon.”

articles.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
articles.summary: Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff…

image.caption: Vladimir Putin, seeking to to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine? Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP

blocks.text: The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

blocks.caption: The radar near Gvardeysk would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications, detect aircraft movements and ballistic missilesImage: Planet Labs

blocks.text: The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.
Mass surveillance system

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.
"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.
"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.
"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.
Russia ramps up drone war with new launch megabase
Electronic warfare hub

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.
"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.
The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

blocks.caption: This satellite image shows what might be another large circular antenna complex near the city of ChernyakhovskImage: Planet Labs PBC

blocks.text: ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

blocks.caption: With airfields like Chkalovsk, Russia is beefing up its military presence in KaliningradImage: Planet Labs PBC

blocks.text: "These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."
Motivation for the West

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.
"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."
Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.
The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?
